claim_status_semantics: claim_status uses the canonical Claim Schema v1.0 statuses: EXPLICIT | INFERRED | UNKNOWN. INFERRED claims are project/AI interpretation, never presented as direct source statements.

claims.ambiguity_notes: Range boundary definition is not pinned by the source.
claims.observability_missing_inputs: none; 'middle of a trading range' requires an interpreted range boundary (INFERRED), not an unavailable input
claims.source_context_note: Explicit no-trade/entry-location rule: do not put capital to work in the middle of a trading range; buy new highs or pullbacks.
claims.source_excerpt_short_or_paraphrase: 'The worst thing you can do in terms of market timing is to buy in the middle of a trading range. Either buy new highs, or buy pullbacks, but don't put your capital to work in the middle of a trading range.'
claims.source_observation_surface: price position relative to a trading range

claims.ambiguity_notes: No numeric definition of 'impulse', 'thrust', or the standard-deviation measure.
claims.observability_missing_inputs: 'increase in standard deviation' is not pinned (measure/window undefined); the other cues are price-observable
claims.source_context_note: Explicit cue list for move initiation; several components are price-based (range expansion, breakaway gap, failure to make a lower low); 'increase in standard deviation' is not defined by the source.
claims.source_excerpt_short_or_paraphrase: 'Moves often start in either direction with an impulse and a thrust. It may be a range expansion, an increase in standard deviation, a breakaway gap, or even a failure to make a lower low.'
claims.source_observation_surface: price bars / range / gaps / lower-low failure

claims.ambiguity_notes: Swing-low identification is not pinned; ADX parameters are explicit (14-period).
claims.observability_missing_inputs: indicators are derivable from owned OHLCV; 'newly formed swing low' requires an interpreted swing definition (INFERRED)
claims.source_context_note: Explicit, structured pullback-in-trend rules. Indicator-based (ADX, EMA); both are computable from OHLC but are indicators, not raw price/volume/session.
claims.source_excerpt_short_or_paraphrase: Holy Grail buy rules (sells reversed): 1. The 14-period ADX must initially be greater than 30 and rising. 2. Look for a retracement in price to the 20-period exponential moving average, usually accompanied by a turndown in ADX. 3. When price touches the 20-period moving average, put a buy stop above the high of the previous bar. 4. Once filled, enter a protective sell stop at the newly formed swing low. Trail stops as profits grow.
claims.source_observation_surface: ADX (OHLC-derived), 20-period EMA, bar highs, swing lows

claims.ambiguity_notes: 'does not fill the gap' is explicit but tick-level fill semantics need a defined project convention.
claims.observability_missing_inputs: none for raw bars; gap 'unfilled' semantics are explicit
claims.source_context_note: Explicit gap-reversal rules; fully price/bar-based (gaps from OHLC). Single-article mention; no commodity-futures anchor.
claims.source_excerpt_short_or_paraphrase: Three-Day Unfilled Gap Reversals: 1. Today the security gaps lower and does not fill the gap. 2. Over the next three trading sessions, have in place a buy stop one tick above the high of the gap-down day. 3. If filled, place a protective sell stop at the low of the gap-down day. 4. Protect any accrued profits with a trailing stop. 5. If not filled after three trading sessions, cancel the initial buy stop.
claims.source_observation_surface: gaps, bar highs/lows, session days

claims.ambiguity_notes: Point selection (what counts as a swing top/bottom) is not mechanically defined.
claims.observability_missing_inputs: swing point identification and trendline drawing are discretionary; no objective selection rule is pinned
claims.source_context_note: Explicit construction rules but the source describes recognition as a trained-eye skill ('you will automatically get a magically trained eye'). Discretionary pattern identification.
claims.source_excerpt_short_or_paraphrase: Wolfe Wave construction: wave 2 is the top of a bar chart; wave 3 is the bottom of the first decline after wave 2; wave 1 is the bottom prior to the wave 2 top (point 3 lower than point 1); wave 4 is the top of wave 3; a trend line from point 1 to point 3 projects to the anticipated reversal point (wave 5), the entry point; price objective from a trendline from points 1 to 4; initial stop just beneath point 5, then moved to break-even.
claims.source_observation_surface: bar swing points, trendlines

claims.ambiguity_notes: NR7 is attributed lineage (Toby Crabel contraction/expansion); breakout entry 'with the volatility' has no explicit volume threshold.
claims.observability_missing_inputs: none (bar ranges and breakout levels from OHLCV); instrument transfer to Chinese futures is INFERRED, not explicit
claims.source_context_note: Explicit NR7 definition (narrowest range of the last seven days) and an explicit entry: buy the breakout of the NR7 day, going with the volatility. Chart example is September Cocoa (commodity futures). KEY claim for the selected family.
claims.source_excerpt_short_or_paraphrase: 'A good example might be buying the breakout of an NR7 day, which stands for a narrow range seven-day pattern ... That trade would be going with the volatility in that case.' (Figure: 'A narrow range seven-day (NR7) in today's trading range is the narrowest trading range in the last seven days. The low volatility leads to a trend.')
claims.source_observation_surface: daily bar ranges, breakout of NR7 day high/low

claims.ambiguity_notes: 'breakout mode' vs 'swing mode' selection is discretionary; no objective classifier is given.
claims.observability_missing_inputs: none (prior-day high/low from OHLCV; session/calendar metadata governs day boundaries)
claims.source_context_note: Explicit prior-day-level reference framework: previous day's high/low are the most important reference points; the trader decides the day before whether to trade that market in breakout mode or swing/countertrend mode.
claims.source_excerpt_short_or_paraphrase: 'I write down the previous day's high and low, because to me those are the most important reference points when I'm entering a position the next day; I like to know where the price today is relative to the previous day's high/low ... I program myself to either being in a breakout or countertrend mode.'
claims.source_observation_surface: prior-day high/low, current price relative to them

claims.ambiguity_notes: Slope ('declining'/'rising') definition is not pinned.
claims.observability_missing_inputs: ADX is computable from owned OHLCV; 'declining'/'rising' slope semantics not pinned
claims.source_context_note: Explicit no-trade/filter rules keyed to ADX. Indicator-based (ADX computable from OHLC) but an indicator, and 'declining'/'rising' are not numerically defined.
claims.source_excerpt_short_or_paraphrase: 'I avoid the markets where the ADX falls below 20 and is declining, because there's just not enough movement between the swings for me. Likewise, I have something of a golden rule: I will not fade a market. I will not try to trade against a market where the ADX is above 32 and rising.'
claims.source_observation_surface: ADX (OHLC-derived)

claims.ambiguity_notes: 'if there is a trend' is not objectively defined here.
claims.observability_missing_inputs: EMA computable from OHLCV; 'trend' and 'pullback' semantics not pinned
claims.source_context_note: Explicit pullback-in-trend entry framework using a 20-period EMA. Indicator-based but EMA is computable from owned OHLC.
claims.source_excerpt_short_or_paraphrase: 'If there is a trend, I'll try to always look for buying a pullback to a moving average ... I personally use a 20-period exponential moving average on all my markets.'
claims.source_observation_surface: 20-period EMA, price pullback

claims.ambiguity_notes: 'peters out' and 'big day' are qualitative.
claims.observability_missing_inputs: 'trend day' needs the source's trend-day definition (see C-RAS-012); otherwise daily bars are observable
claims.source_context_note: Explicit multi-day structure claim (test of prior low, trend day, peter out) with an explicit management implication (carry a good trend day overnight for follow-through).
claims.source_excerpt_short_or_paraphrase: 'Most likely what'll happen is that the first day the market makes a test of the previous day's low. Then the middle day is when it'll have a trend day, and then the third day it peters out. Usually the middle day tends to be the big day, so if you ever get a middle, or a good trend day, or a good movement that day you should always carry that trade overnight because the odds are that you will get follow through the next day.'
claims.source_observation_surface: daily price structure relative to prior day's low; trend-day character

claims.ambiguity_notes: 'range expansion' and 'steady pattern' are not numerically pinned.
claims.observability_missing_inputs: none (open/close/high/low from 1-min OHLCV; session metadata governs day boundaries)
claims.source_context_note: Explicit trend-day definition. Purely price-based (open/close/range/sequence of highs and lows). KEY claim for the selected family. Note: 'in the index futures' indicates the base instrument scope.
claims.source_excerpt_short_or_paraphrase: 'A trend day opens on one end of its range and closes on the opposite end, has range expansion, and makes a steady pattern of higher highs and higher lows, or vice versa, throughout the day. In the index futures, there are two or three trend days a month.'
claims.source_observation_surface: daily open/close/range, sequence of intraday highs/lows

claims.ambiguity_notes: 'significant degree' and 'large opening gap' are not numerically pinned.
claims.observability_missing_inputs: none (all from OHLCV + session metadata)
claims.source_context_note: Explicit trend-day precursor conditions. NR7 (narrowest range of past seven bars) is explicitly defined here and in the 1993 article. All price/session based. KEY claim for the selected family.
claims.source_excerpt_short_or_paraphrase: Three different types of conditions tend to precede a trend day: first, a significant degree of range contraction, 'such as an NR7 day, which is a bar with the narrowest range of the past seven bars'; second, a trend day after a large opening gap; finally, if the market is approaching new 20-day highs or lows, 'these points tend to be magnets or key chart levels that will accelerate price action.'
claims.source_observation_surface: daily bar ranges (NR7), opening gaps, 20-day highs/lows

claims.ambiguity_notes: 'very large' 15-min bar and 'significant increase' in volume are not numerically pinned; breadth input unavailable.
claims.observability_missing_inputs: breadth (NYSE advancing/declining) is NOT_OBSERVABLE_WITH_CURRENT_DATA; no OHLCV proxy is authorized
claims.source_context_note: Explicit trend-day confirmation mix. Volume and session components are observable; breadth (advancing minus declining) is a US equity-market surface NOT owned by the Chinese-futures corpus. The confirmation is a handicap, not the NR7 bracket entry trigger itself.
claims.source_excerpt_short_or_paraphrase: Trend-day confirmation: 'a very large 15-minute bar to open the trading session' (attributed to Toby Crabel); volume increase ('Which of those stocks have had a significant increase in volume in the first 15 minutes relative to the past two weeks?'); leadership (IBM/Microsoft/Intel/GE); trendiness 10-10:30/10:45; and 'the last and most important thing is that I want to see trend in the market breadth - the difference between advancing issues and declining issues.'
claims.source_observation_surface: opening 15-min bar, volume, session time, breadth (advancing minus declining)

claims.ambiguity_notes: The bracket entry is explicit; instrument transfer to Chinese futures is INFERRED (the practice statement is in an index-futures context).
claims.observability_missing_inputs: none (session range from governed session metadata + 1-min OHLCV); choosing 45-min vs 1-hour is a source-permitted window choice, not an invented threshold
claims.source_context_note: Explicit self-contained entry/management practice: the day after an NR7 day, bracket stops around the early morning range (either the first 45 minutes or the first hour - the source states both worked in her own test). Price/session based; no breadth/TICK required for the entry. KEY claim for the selected family. Base instrument in context is index futures.
claims.source_excerpt_short_or_paraphrase: 'Something I'll almost always do the day after an NR7 day is bracket stops around the early morning range. When I tested this out about five years ago, it didn't matter whether you bracketed the first 45 minutes range or the first hour's range. If there's going to be a trend day, you're going to catch it.'
claims.source_observation_surface: NR7 day, next-day early morning range (45-min or 1-hour), bracket stop levels

claims.ambiguity_notes: Signal/tendency only; management/exit/target not pinned in the article; 'widest range of the past four days' is explicit.
claims.observability_missing_inputs: none (bar ranges/closes from OHLCV)
claims.source_context_note: Explicit wide-range-bar tendency/signal. Purely price-based (bar ranges and closes). Single-article mention; no explicit stop/exit/target structure is given in the article.
claims.source_excerpt_short_or_paraphrase: 'If today has the widest range of the past four days and an up close, the odds the low of the bar will be taken out in the next two days is the least-probable scenario ... If there was a down-closing wide-range bar and the market takes out the high of that bar within two days, it's a buy signal, because that's the least-probable scenario - it occurs maybe 20 percent of the time.'
claims.source_observation_surface: daily bar ranges, closes, two-day takeout of high/low

claims.ambiguity_notes: 'volatility extreme' and 'V-spike reversal' are not numerically pinned.
claims.observability_missing_inputs: volatility is computable from OHLCV; flag pattern identification is visual/discretionary and not mechanically pinned
claims.source_context_note: Explicit no-trade/failure condition: continuation flags (bull/bear) are unreliable at volatility extremes and in contracting volatility; a volatility filter is required. Also: 'If I simply [stop trading the pattern] after we've had a big move, it will eliminate the system's drawdown periods.'
claims.source_excerpt_short_or_paraphrase: 'Bull and bear flags ... work in normal market conditions. But a bear flag, for example, will fail after a volatility extreme like a V-spike reversal because the market will likely make a spike and ledge instead of making a good retest back down. So, shorting the reaction after a V-spike reversal is a sucker's play. Flags will also fail when there's no volatility ... Statistical reliability only comes with a volatility filter.'
claims.source_observation_surface: volatility condition, flag patterns (visual)

claims.ambiguity_notes: 'strong reading' threshold is deliberately rough in source.
claims.observability_missing_inputs: ROC computable from OHLCV; the 'strong' comparison window (3-4 weeks) is a rough source quantification, not a pinned threshold
claims.source_context_note: Explicit momentum pullback cue using a two-period ROC (difference between current close and close two bars ago); 'strong' is roughly quantified as greater than readings over the previous three to four weeks. Indicator (ROC) is a price derivative computable from owned closes.
claims.source_excerpt_short_or_paraphrase: On the two-period rate of change (ROC) momentum: 'Typically, after two strong readings in an uptrend, [a pullback will occur].' A strong reading is 'one that's greater than the readings over the previous three to four weeks. It sort of depends on the individual market and environment, but three to four weeks is a rough way to quantify it.'
claims.source_observation_surface: two-period ROC (closes)

claims.ambiguity_notes: Trend-context and 'early' definitions not pinned.
claims.observability_missing_inputs: gaps/session observable; 'down-trending market' definition not pinned
claims.source_context_note: Explicit conditional entry rule (early gap up in a down-trending market -> short). 'Down-trending market' is not objectively defined; 'early gap up' needs a session-time definition.
claims.source_excerpt_short_or_paraphrase: 'In a down-trending market, an early gap up is a short 95 percent of the time.'
claims.source_observation_surface: gap, session time, market trend context

claims.ambiguity_notes: Counterexample/process claim.
claims.observability_missing_inputs: ADX computable; 'guessing' is a process failure mode, not a market-scene input
claims.source_context_note: Explicit failure/counterexample: guessing a breakout direction is unreliable; the source uses this as an argument for defined statistics/strategies and a low-ADX warning against guessing. Useful failure/no-trade evidence.
claims.source_excerpt_short_or_paraphrase: 'If I try to guess a breakout, I'm wrong 90 percent of the time. I'm a perfect contrary indicator. ... I just know if it's a low ADX, I'm going to be wrong if I try to guess.'
claims.source_observation_surface: breakout guessing / low-ADX context

claims.ambiguity_notes: Qualitative management; relevant to the selected family's exit semantics.
claims.observability_missing_inputs: price observable; 'gives back more than it should' and 'price objective' are not numerically pinned
claims.source_context_note: Explicit management/exit principles for held positions: exit on the first reaction/pause when price gives back more than it should; take at least half off at a price objective when continuation is uncertain. Qualitative; not numerically pinned.
claims.source_excerpt_short_or_paraphrase: 'The minute the market gives back more than it should, you get out on the first reaction or pause.' Also: 'If the market reaches a price objective, and you're really not sure if it's going to continue, you have to at least take half the position off.'
claims.source_observation_surface: price behavior vs objective/expectation

claims.ambiguity_notes: Specific percentages are the source's own stated tendency; not a trading rule by itself.
claims.observability_missing_inputs: none (bar ranges/closes from OHLCV)
claims.source_context_note: Explicit, quantified bar-close-position tendency. Purely price-based (bar close position in range, next-bar high/close). Illustrates the source's tendency-modeling style; no entry/exit rules are attached here.
claims.source_excerpt_short_or_paraphrase: 'Let's take the example of a daily S&P bar that closes in the upper 20 percent of its range. The odds are approximately 75 percent that the next bar will trade above the high of this bar, but there's only a 50-percent chance it will close above it. In other words, the pattern forecasts the market should trade above the most recent day's high, but it has no forecasting value regarding the close.'
claims.source_observation_surface: daily bar close position, next-bar high/close

claims.ambiguity_notes: The source explicitly allows multiple contraction proxies; NR7 is one pinned example.
claims.observability_missing_inputs: contraction is measurable from OHLCV but the source gives no single pinned method ('a number of different proxies you can use')
claims.source_context_note: Explicit framework claim: measuring market contraction tells the trader to switch to a breakout mode. This is the conceptual umbrella for the NR7 / range-contraction -> trend-day breakout family. The specific method is discretionary observation.
claims.source_excerpt_short_or_paraphrase: 'I use different measurements for the amount of contraction in the market. There's a number of different proxies you can use, but everybody should have some method of measuring the amount of contraction in the market. Many times, oscillators or momentum indicators will lose their oscillations or extreme readings. This is what I like to measure, and that tells me to switch to a breakout mode.'
claims.source_observation_surface: contraction (bar ranges / oscillator extreme-loss)

claims.ambiguity_notes: Confirmation/handicap input; not part of the NR7 bracket entry itself.
claims.observability_missing_inputs: NYSE TICK / TRIN breadth surface; not owned by the corpus; no OHLCV proxy is authorized
claims.source_context_note: Explicit observability boundary: the source uses NYSE TICK (up-ticking minus down-ticking NYSE stocks) as a momentum oscillator and for trend confirmation. NYSE TICK is NOT owned by the Chinese-futures 1-minute OHLCV corpus and is not ordinary volume; no OHLCV proxy is authorized.
claims.source_excerpt_short_or_paraphrase: 'I use the TICKs like a momentum oscillator: If the TICKs are making new highs, I'll look to buy the pullbacks. ... The bottoms of sell-offs will be accompanied by negative TICK extremes, like -1,000, for example. Tops are characterized much more by complacency, with a lack of TICK readings.'
claims.source_observation_surface: NYSE TICK / breadth (up-ticking minus down-ticking NYSE stocks)

claims.ambiguity_notes: Context/handicap input for the index-futures context; not required for the selected family's core price/session inputs.
claims.observability_missing_inputs: European index data (DAX/EuroStoxx) and US corpus cross-market surface; not owned
claims.source_context_note: Explicit observability boundary: the source uses cross-market leading relationships (DAX/EuroStoxx vs US). Cross-market data is NOT owned by the current Chinese-futures corpus; no proxy is authorized. This is a secondary context input, not part of the NR7/trend-day core entry.
claims.source_excerpt_short_or_paraphrase: 'What you'll find is, if you pull up a 15-minute EuroStoxx chart in the morning, and let's say the chart looked like this (she points to a strongly uptrending chart), I could just buy the S&P futures right then and have [very high odds of a] winning trade because the two markets are so highly correlated.' (DAX/EuroStoxx leading the US markets.)
claims.source_observation_surface: cross-market index relationships (DAX / EuroStoxx vs US)
